claims.text: Cr-containing Fe-Cr-Mo low-alloy steels form a nanoscale Cr2O3 passive film under the stated corrosive conditions.
The Cr2O3 passive film forms preferentially in Cr-enriched regions.
The Cr2O3 passive film is continuous and robust.
The Cr2O3 passive film is the primary barrier responsible for reduced corrosion.
The passive film reduces corrosion by inhibiting ionic transport.
The passive film reduces corrosion by inhibiting metal dissolution.
Increasing alloy chromium content promotes spontaneous formation of a continuous Cr2O3 passive film.
Increasing alloy chromium content promotes formation of an adherent Cr2O3 passive film.
Grain boundaries and other microstructural features may enhance or disrupt passive-film formation.
Higher-Cr steels will form more continuous and better-adhered Cr2O3 films than lower-Cr baseline steels.
Higher-Cr steels will exhibit lower corrosion current densities than lower-Cr baseline steels under otherwise identical conditions.
Higher-Cr steels will exhibit less frequent pitting than lower-Cr baseline steels under otherwise identical conditions.
Passive-film integrity will correlate positively with corrosion resistance.
Lower-Cr baseline steels will form discontinuous or defective passive films.
Lower-Cr baseline steels will have higher corrosion rates under the same exposure conditions.
Lower-Cr baseline steels will undergo more frequent pitting under the same exposure conditions.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply in chloride-rich aqueous environments at approximately pH 4–7 and 60–100°C with controlled oxygen.
The proposed behavior may not apply outside the stated environmental range or to drastically different steel compositions or processing methods.
